t.7.57.1: Having sent that entire army on ahead, Śatrughna, after staying only a month on the road, then went on quickly, alone and in haste.
t.7.57.2: Having stayed two nights along the way, the valiant delight of the Rāghavas went to the holy hermitage of Vālmīki, a most excellent dwelling.
t.7.57.3: He, having saluted the great-souled Vālmīki, best of sages, then joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
t.7.57.5: Having heard the words of Śatrughna, the foremost of sages smiled and replied to the great-souled one: "Welcome to you, O greatly renowned one!"
t.7.57.4: Blessed one, I have come here on my elder's business and wish to stay the night. Tomorrow at daybreak I shall set out for the western quarter, the region of Varuṇa.
t.7.57.7: Then, having accepted the honour, Kākutstha ate the meal of fruits and roots and attained the highest satisfaction.
t.7.57.6: This hermitage, gentle one, belongs to your own family, the line of the Rāghavas. Accept from me without hesitation a seat, water for your feet, and the guest-offering.
t.7.57.8: Having eaten, the mighty-armed one spoke to that great sage: "Whose was this sacrificial splendour of former times, here near the hermitage?"
t.7.57.9: Hearing those words of his, Vālmīki spoke: “Śatrughna, listen, and I will tell you whose sacred abode this was in former times.”
t.7.57.10: Your ancestor was a king named Mitrasaha, the son of the great-souled Sudāsa, valiant and exceedingly righteous.
t.7.57.11: While still a boy, Saudāsa set out on a hunt, and that valiant one saw a pair of Rākṣasas roaming restlessly about.
t.7.57.12: Taking the form of tigers, the two dreadful ones devoured beasts by many thousands, yet, never content, they did not reach satiety.
t.7.57.13: But he, seeing those two Rākṣasas and the forest made empty of game, was seized by great anger and slew one of them with a mighty arrow.
t.7.57.14: Having struck down that one, Saudāsa, bull among men, free of anxiety and with his anger gone, gazed upon the slain demon.
t.7.57.15: Seeing him gazing on, the companion of that rākṣasa was seized by dreadful anguish and spoke these words to Saudāsa.
t.7.57.16: Since you have slain my companion, who had done no wrong, I too shall pay you back in return, O most wicked one.
t.7.57.17: Having spoken thus to him, the rakṣas vanished right there. Then, in the due course of time, the king became Mitrasaha.
t.7.57.18: The king, too, performed a sacrifice near his hermitage, the great horse sacrifice, the Aśvamedha, and Vasiṣṭha watched over it.
t.7.57.20: Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the rākṣasa, remembering his former enmity, took on the form of Vasiṣṭha and spoke thus to the king.
t.7.57.19: There a great sacrifice took place, lasting for many myriads of years. Rich with supreme splendour, it became equal to a sacrifice of the gods.
t.7.57.21: "Today, at the close of the sacrifice, let food with meat be given to me quickly; there should be no hesitation in this matter."
t.7.57.22: Having heard those words spoken by the rākṣasa who could assume any form at will, the lord of the earth spoke to the one skilled in the preparation of food.
t.7.57.23: Act quickly, so that the meal turns out fit for oblation, prepared with meat and savoury, in such a way that the guru may be fully satisfied.
t.7.57.24: At the command of the lord of kings, the cook was bewildered in mind; and then that Rākṣasa once again assumed the guise of the cook there.
t.7.57.25: Then he presented human flesh to the king, saying: "This delicious sacrificial fare and food with meat have been brought."
t.7.57.26: O tiger among men, together with his wife Madayantī, he offered Vasiṣṭha food mixed with meat that had been brought by the rākṣasa.
t.7.57.27: When the brahmin learned that the meat brought to him as food was human flesh, he was seized by great anger and began to speak.
t.7.57.28: Since you wish to give me this food, O king, this very food shall be yours; of this there is no doubt.
t.7.57.29: Then the king, together with his wife, bowing down again and again, told Vasiṣṭha once more what had been said by the one who had taken the form of a brahmin.
t.7.57.30: Hearing that from the lord of kings, and learning of the mischief wrought by the rākṣasa, Vasiṣṭha spoke again to the king, that bull among men.
t.7.57.31: These words that I uttered while overcome by anger cannot be made void, but I will grant you a boon.
t.7.57.33: Thus that king, the crusher of foes, having endured that curse to its end, regained his kingdom once more and protected his subjects.
t.7.57.32: The term of this curse shall be twelve years, and by my grace, O lord of kings, you will not remember what has passed.
t.7.57.35: Having heard that most dreadful story of the lord of kings, and having saluted the great sage, he entered the leaf-thatched hut.
t.7.57.34: Here, near this hermitage, lies the auspicious site of the sacrifice of that Kalmāṣapāda, about which you ask, O Rāghava.
